summary: Michael Hablich, product manager for Chrome DevTools at Google, presents engineering lessons from building Chrome DevTools for agents as an MCP server. The tool works with any MCP-capable agent harness including Gemini CLI, Cloud Code, Codex, and Open Claw. The team shipped it because coding agents were flying blind — generating code but unable to validate results. Their first attempt threw raw trace files (50,000 lines of JSON, multiple megabytes) at agents, which blew through context windows. The fix was semantic summaries in markdown, pointing agents at the right information rather than forcing them to read the entire trace. A key conceptual insight: agents are a separate user class. They share intent and goals with humans but think differently with different cognitive bottlenecks — humans need visual complexity while agents need different representations. Hablich distinguishes effectiveness (does the agent complete the user journey?) from efficiency (token cost, tool calls, duration). The metric tokens per successful outcome measures interface fuel efficiency, with two caveats: efficiency is worthless without effectiveness, and metrics vary dramatically across user journeys so should be compared within journeys, not globally. The team addresses token burn from three angles: tool categorization (hiding niche tools behind CLI parameters), slim mode (exposing only three tools with a trade-off of potentially requiring extra turns), and a CLI interface enabling command chaining for local post-processing. Error recovery is addressed as a spectrum: useful error messages rewritten to enable agent self-healing, proactive detours to counteract model training data, and diagnostic playbooks for setup issues. Discoverability is the fourth pillar. The team initially had one monolithic tool, debug_webpage, which failed because agents could not compose behaviors. Decomposing it into 25 tools shifted the problem to tool selection. Citing research that 97% of MCP tool descriptions have quality smells, Hablich emphasizes that the schema is the UI for the agent. Best practices include defining clear purpose and activation criteria with keywords agents can connect to (e.g., LCP, INP, CLS for performance), while trading off context window size and smaller model bias. Skills can supercharge workflows but are not free lunch — too many shift the problem rather than solve it. Finally, trust boundaries matter: the autoconnect feature deliberately keeps human-consent friction by design to prevent backdoors, informed by Simon Willison's lethal trifecta. Three tiers of browsing agents require different trust models: local dev with human-in-loop consent, CI with data separation, and full internet access requiring prompt injection mitigations and domain allow lists. Four final takeaways: measure fuel efficiency with tokens per successful outcome, turn errors into recovery playbooks, audit descriptions for intent, and never compromise trust for convenience.

sections.title: Introduction and Demo
sections.summary: Hablich introduces himself as Chrome DevTools PM at Google and demos the MCP server working with Gemini CLI for performance tracing, noting compatibility with any MCP-capable agent harness.

sections.title: Problem: Agents Flying Blind and Trace File Overload
sections.summary: Coding agents could generate code but not validate results. Raw trace files (50,000 lines of JSON) blew through context windows. The team fixed this by returning markdown semantic summaries instead, pointing agents at the right information.

sections.title: Agents as a Different User Class and Effectiveness vs Efficiency
sections.summary: Agents share human intent but have different cognitive bottlenecks. Effectiveness means completing the user journey; efficiency means minimizing token cost, tool calls, and duration. Tokens per successful outcome measures fuel efficiency, with caveats about requiring effectiveness and not comparing globally across user journeys.

sections.title: Reducing Token Burn
sections.summary: Three approaches: tool categorization hides niche tools behind CLI parameters; slim mode exposes only three tools with a trade-off in capability; CLI interface enables command chaining for local post-processing, saving tokens by avoiding model processing.

sections.title: Error Recovery
sections.summary: Error recovery is a spectrum: useful error messages rewritten for agent self-healing, proactive detours to counteract model training data, and diagnostic playbooks as skills for setup issues. All increase agent harness resilience.

sections.title: Discoverability and Tool Design
sections.summary: The initial monolithic debug_webpage tool failed because agents could not compose behaviors. Decomposing it into 25 tools shifted the problem to tool selection. Citing research that 97% of MCP tool descriptions have quality smells, Hablich stresses that the schema is the UI for the agent. Best practices include defining clear purpose and activation criteria with keywords agents can connect to, while trading off context window size and smaller model bias. Skills can supercharge workflows but too many shift the problem rather than solve it.

sections.title: Trust, Autoconnect, and Security Tiers
sections.summary: Chrome DevTools for Agents has an autoconnect feature for screen sharing with agents. Users requested removing the consent friction, but the team kept it by design to prevent backdoors, informed by Simon Willison's lethal trifecta. Three tiers of browsing agents require different trust models: local dev with human-in-loop consent, CI with data separation via containers and separate profiles, and full internet access requiring prompt injection mitigations and domain allow lists. Hablich concludes with four takeaways: measure fuel efficiency with tokens per successful outcome, turn errors into recovery playbooks, audit descriptions for intent, and never compromise trust for convenience.
